leads.title: How the Architecture of Sound Is Transforming Cities
leads.summary: B efore Chris Downey lost his sight, he had a wind chime on his front porch. After he became blind, he realized that he could listen out for it to help him find his way home. But after a few years, his nextdoor neighbor added a wind chime to their porch. And then the neighbor on the other side, just uphill, added a chime of their own. “Three in a row!” Downey said. He assumed at this point that his chime would no longer be able to help him locate his house. But then he noticed that the chime that the neighbor up the hill had hung was slightly higher in pitch compared to his own, and the neighbor who lived slightly downhill had hung lower, deeper chimes. “It was completely coincidental,” Downey said. “But they were perfectly sonified to match the topographic condition.” Downey had worked as an architect for 20 years before he became blind in 2008, and this chorus of wind chimes suggested a new direction in his work: The sounds of the city weren’t just decorative, musical — they could define the physical contours of a space as dramatically as a concrete wall or an open door to the street. Chris Downey played a significant role in the design of the Salesforce Transit Center in San Francisco. Credit: Engel Ching / Shutterstock He began developing a set of design principles that understood architectural accessibility not only in terms of wheelchair ramps and braille on elevator buttons, but ones that considered the ways that sound (and other senses) shaped the experience of blind and other disabled people navigating the built environment. He became part of an evolving conversation in inclusive design that expanded the idea of access, and reconsidered the place of the disabled body in public space. leads.title: Karnataka Plans to Revive 500 Lakes: What Does a Truly Healthy Lake Look Like?
leads.summary: For a city built around lakes, Bengaluru has spent years trying to answer: how do you bring a lake back? The answer usually lies with the physical things that are easiest to see: remove the silt, repair the bund, clear the weeds, fix the feeder channel, and make the edges accessible. Now, Karnataka is preparing to do this at scale. The state has drawn up a Rs 150-crore plan to rejuvenate 500 lakes across seven water-stressed districts, PTI reported on 22 September 2026. Of these, 135 are in Bengaluru Urban and Bengaluru Rural.   The proposed works include desilting, strengthening and raising bunds, repairing canals and feeder channels, and beautification. The project is planned with World Bank assistance. The 500 lakes are spread across Bengaluru Rural (68), Bengaluru Urban (67), Bidar (44), Chikkaballapur (90), Kalaburagi (49), Tumakuru (96) and Kolar (86). But Bengaluru’s experience with its restored lakes suggests that bringing back water is only one part of bringing back a lake . So, what should a healthy urban lake actually look like? There are at least three tests. The first test: What enters the lake? Stand beside a Bengaluru lake, and the first thing to ask is: what is flowing into it? Historically, Bengaluru’s lakes formed a connected cascade. Water moved from one tank to another across the city’s natural terrain. The World Bank’s 2025 technical assessment of the Karnataka Water Security and Resilience Programme describes the remaining lake network as having the potential to help the city manage both floods and droughts. But that function depends on the quality and quantity of water entering the system. leads.title: The Elephant 'Hug' Went Viral. Here's What the Veterinarian Says It Really Meant
leads.summary: The Teesta was carrying the calf away. Near Spur Number 12, in the Malbazar subdivision of Jalpaiguri district in Bengal, a few fishermen noticed the tiny elephant being pulled along by the river's current. It was barely a few days old and had already been separated from its herd. The fishermen were out on the river when they saw it struggling in the water. They turned their boat towards the calf and followed it through the current for nearly three kilometres before they could reach it. By then, the calf had travelled several kilometres from where its herd had attempted to cross the Teesta. They pulled it into the boat. In the video that followed, the exhausted calf is seen being held close by the fishermen. For many people watching the footage, the image looked unmistakably like a hug. The moment has since travelled far beyond the river. Shared widely on social media, it has drawn praise for the fishermen who went after the calf and for the forest officials who helped reunite it with its mother. For a newborn elephant calf, the Teesta River became a terrifying journey away from his mother. Only 3–4 days old, he was swept nearly 5 km downstream by the river’s powerful currents while crossing with his mother. And when a calf appears to embrace the people rescuing it, is that really what is happening?
